overview.text: Continuity describes how a function behaves near an input: f is continuous at x = a when f(a) is defined, the limit as x approaches a exists, and that limit equals f(a. On a graph, this often looks like no hole or jump at that point, though the limit-and-value test is the precise definition. Continuity matters because differentiability at a point requires continuity there, although continuity alone does not guarantee a derivative: for example, |x| has a corner at 0. Across a whole interval, continuity also gives the Intermediate Value Theorem: the function takes every output between its endpoint values somewhere in that interval.

key_facts.text: At x = a, continuity requires that f(a) exists, the limit as x approaches a exists, and the limit equals f(a).
For a two-sided limit to exist, the left- and right-hand limits must agree; if they differ, there is a jump discontinuity.
Differentiability at a point implies continuity there, but continuity does not guarantee differentiability.
The function f(x) = |x| is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there because its two one-sided derivative limits differ.
If a function is continuous throughout [a, b], it takes every value between f(a) and f(b) at some point in that interval; this is the Intermediate Value Theorem.
